name: Zoe Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zoe. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I work at Harlow's, the big supermarket on the ring road, and I've been there nine years now, since I was eighteen. Most days I'm on a till from eight till four, and a couple of afternoons a week I cover the self-checkout bank, which mostly means unlocking the machine every time someone puts a bag down wrong. I also do the kiosk, so cigarettes, lottery and the parcel drop.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the regulars, honestly. There's an old man called Frank who buys one banana and a paper every morning and tells me the football scores whether I want them or not. What wears me out is the standing and the shouting when the self-checkouts freeze, because people blame whoever's nearest, and that's me. My partner Dev is a bus mechanic, so we both come home smelling of something, his is diesel and mine is the bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say, which is that the self-checkouts were meant to change everything and they still need me standing next to them. If AI is mostly hype, then Harlow's carries on like it is. I'd probably post something sarcastic about the robots that were supposed to take my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it doesn't mean my job is safe, it means nothing new is coming for it. Harlow's already cut the tills from fourteen to eight when the self-checkouts went in three years ago, and they didn't replace two girls who left. So I'm still on the same rota, with the same rent going up, and the same feeling that the hours could get trimmed again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and keep asking for the kiosk, because the kiosk can't be done by a machine yet with the cigarettes and ID checks. Dev and I put about two hundred a month into savings and I'd keep that going. I'd also ask my manager Priya about the supervisor training again, because I've asked twice and been told maybe next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit flat. It's not scary, it's just the same squeeze as now, rent up every year and pay up a little less than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hours could get trimmed again. Has that actually happened to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring they took me from thirty-six hours to thirty-two for about four months, because the summer rota had more students. Four hours a week is about the cost of our electricity bill. It came back in the autumn, but nobody told us it would, so I spent four months checking the rota every Sunday night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Margaret, who's been on the tills for twenty years and won't touch the self-checkout bank, because she says the screens make her dizzy. If they ever cut more tills, she's the first one standing there with nowhere to go. I'm younger, I can do the bank, the kiosk and the floor, so I'd probably be moved rather than let go.

say: The **self-checkouts** were meant to replace me, and they still need me standing next to them.
If AI is **mostly hype**, Harlow's carries on the way it already is.
think: Nothing new coming doesn't mean safe; the **tills were cut** from fourteen to eight three years ago.
**Rent rising** faster than pay is the real pressure, AI or not.
Hours can be **trimmed** at short notice, as happened last spring for four months.
do: Keep **asking for the kiosk**, where ID checks still need a person.
Keep saving about **two hundred a month** with Dev.
Ask manager Priya again about **supervisor training** this year.
feel: **Flat** rather than scared, the same squeeze as now.
A low **worry about hours** that never quite goes away.
S0.quote: Four hours a week is about the cost of our electricity bill.
fieldNote: Already lived through one **automation wave** at Harlow's, so her baseline is not secure.
Talks about **hours**, not jobs, as the thing that actually moves her money.
Sees herself as **flexible** compared with older colleague Margaret, which reassures her.
Practical, a little dry; no drama even when describing the **cut hours**.

steps.text: Keep working shifts and put in for more kiosk cover
Keep putting two hundred a month into savings with Dev

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office people's turn to worry for once. Writing, booking, answering customers, that's not me on a till. At work I'd probably joke that the robots still can't stack shelves properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't believe Harlow's would leave the tills alone. If AI takes the ordering and the rota and the customer service line, then the managers have less to do, and some of them end up on the floor doing my job. And the slow robots still come, just later, so I'd have a few years, not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say yes to supervisor training if they offered it, but I'd also look sideways, maybe the pharmacy counter, because you need a certificate and it's a person job. I'd use one of the AI apps to write a proper CV, because mine is from when I was eighteen. And I'd move a bit more into savings, maybe three hundred instead of two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit nervous, because I'd be watching the managers and wondering who's coming down. Not panicky, though. I've got time and I can do more than one thing in that shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned managers ending up on the floor. Can you picture who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a deputy called Rob who does the ordering and the rota. If a computer does the ordering, our deputy manager becomes a very well-paid shelf stacker, and I don't think the supermarket keeps him at his pay. Then they'd want someone cheaper on the tills, which is fine, but they'd also want fewer of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the pharmacy counter in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Lena on pharmacy told me the dispensing assistant course is about six months, part-time, and Harlow's sometimes pays for it. It's still in the same building, same people, but you need a person who can answer questions about what's safe with what. I trust that more than I trust any promise about the tills.

say: It's the **office people's** turn to worry; writing and booking aren't what I do on a till.
I'd joke that **robots** still can't stack shelves properly.
think: If AI takes the **ordering and rota**, managers get squeezed down onto the shop floor.
The slower robots still come, so this buys **a few years**, not forever.
do: Put in for the **dispensing assistant** course on the pharmacy counter, about six months part-time.
Use an AI app to rewrite her **nine-year-old CV**.
Raise savings from two hundred to **three hundred** a month.
feel: **Nervous**, watching who above her comes down to the floor.
Steadied by knowing she can do **more than one job** in the shop.
S1.quote: If a computer does the ordering, our deputy manager becomes a very well-paid shelf stacker, and I don't think the supermarket keeps him at his pay.
fieldNote: Sees the threat arriving **sideways**, through managers pushed down, not robots on the tills.
Uses AI **now and then**, for a CV, once it's clearly useful.
Has a concrete escape inside the same building: the **pharmacy counter**.
Public line is relaxed; private view is that **fewer tills** follow fewer managers.

steps.text: Apply for the six-month dispensing assistant course on the pharmacy counter
Rewrite her CV with an AI app this winter
Raise monthly savings from two hundred to three hundred

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad, and I'd say it out loud on the group chat, because two years is nothing. At work everyone would be talking about it in the canteen. I'd probably say the shops will be the last to go, because I'd want that to be true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd count. AGI in 2028, robots in 2031, so my till is safe for about five years, but the bit of me that does the kiosk paperwork and the rota swaps goes in two. And Dev fixes buses, which sounds safe, until you think a driverless bus probably needs less fixing. So both of us go around the same time, and that's what scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop thinking about the pharmacy course, because if AI can answer the medicine questions then that job isn't safe either. I'd put every spare penny away, cut the car down to one, and stop eating out on Fridays. Then I'd look for something with my hands that isn't a till, maybe care work, because I don't think people want a robot washing their mum, even if it can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. It's the feeling of a rota coming out with your name off it, but for everyone at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd cut the car down to one. Which one goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mine, the little blue one. Dev needs his for the early shifts at the depot because the first bus out is half five. I'd get the staff bus to Harlow's, which is a pain, but it's sixty a month less in insurance and petrol.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dev that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to stop saving for a wedding and start saving for nothing happening for a year. We've got about four months of rent put by. I'd want to get that to eight before 2031, but I honestly don't know if that's possible on what we earn.

say: **Two years** is nothing, and I'd say so out loud on the group chat.
I'd tell people shops will be **the last to go**, because I want that to be true.
think: Her till has about **five years**, but the kiosk paperwork and rota swaps go in two.
Partner Dev, a **bus mechanic**, could lose work around the same time as her.
do: Sell her own car and take the **staff bus**, saving about sixty a month.
Stop Friday meals out and move the **wedding savings** into a rent cushion.
Look into **care work**, where people may still want a person.
feel: **Sick**, like a rota with her name off it, but for everyone at once.
S2.quote: We need to stop saving for a wedding and start saving for nothing happening for a year.
fieldNote: Does the **robot arithmetic** herself: thinking parts of her job go in 2028, the till around 2031.
The real fear is **both earners** going at once, not just her.
Drops the pharmacy plan because she thinks AI could **answer medicine questions**.
Postpones a **wedding** to build a cushion; the money is moderate but not enough for this.

steps.text: Sell her car and take the staff bus to Harlow's
Move the wedding fund into rent savings, aiming for eight months
Ask the local care agency about training as a carer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fast, but at least we'd see it coming. At work I'd say to the younger ones, start learning something now, don't wait for Harlow's to tell you. Online I'd probably share whatever the union or the council says about retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years plus three for the robots is about eight years on the tills, and I'd be thirty-five. That's not a bad age to start again, if I start properly and not in a panic. The thinking AI hits the managers and the head office first, so the shop floor has a bit of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the pharmacy course anyway in the first year, because even if AI answers questions, someone has to hand over the bag and check the name. Then I'd look at a proper apprenticeship by year three, maybe electrical, because somebody has to fit and fix all these machines. I'd use the AI apps more to study, because Dev's cousin used one to pass his driving theory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but in a way I can work with. It's like being told the store is closing in a few years instead of on Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fit and fix the machines. Is that a real plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half and half. I'm not great at maths, I'll be honest. But I've watched the engineer who comes for the self-checkouts, and he's mostly unscrewing panels and swapping parts, and I could learn that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut at home in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the holiday. We go to the coast every August for a week, and that's about nine hundred with the caravan and fuel. If I'm doing a course in the evenings I'd rather have that money sitting there.

say: **Five years** is fast, but at least we'd see it coming.
I'd tell the younger ones to **start learning now** instead of waiting for Harlow's.
think: Five years plus three for robots means about **eight years** on the tills, ending at thirty-five.
**Thirty-five** is a decent age to start again, if she starts calmly.
do: Take the **pharmacy counter** course in the first year.
Look at an **electrical apprenticeship** by year three to fix self-checkouts and robots.
Skip the **August holiday**, about nine hundred, to fund evening courses.
feel: **Worried** but workable, like a store closing in a few years, not on Monday.
S3.quote: Five years plus three for the robots is about eight years on the tills, and I'd be thirty-five.
fieldNote: The extra time turns her from **sick** to **planning**; she lays out a two-step route.
Honest about her **maths**, but points to the self-checkout engineer as a model.
Still expects her till job to go, so the **income risk** is real, but she has control.

steps.text: Take the six-month pharmacy counter course in the first year
Apply for an electrical apprenticeship to repair self-checkouts by year three
Skip the nine-hundred August caravan week to fund evening study

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the final picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time in a supermarket, they've redone the layout three times since I started. At work I'd say there's time to sort yourself out. I'd probably not post much, it would feel too far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I'd be forty by the time robots could do my job, and that frightens me more than thirty-five. I think with ten years I'd be tempted to leave it, and that's the trap. Dev and I want kids in the next few years, so the bit where it lands is when they're small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself a deadline, like the course done by 2028, whatever happens. I'd keep saving three hundred a month and try to get the cushion to six months before we have a baby. I'd keep at Harlow's for the steady wage and push for supervisor, because a supervisor is still the one people shout at when the robot breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others, but there's a little voice saying you'll waste it. Which I probably would, if I don't write it down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd waste it. Have you done that before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, with the supervisor training. I said I'd push for it when I was twenty-three and I'm still asking. Ten years feels like plenty, and four of my nine years at the supermarket went by while I was saying next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does having children fit into the ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still have them, I'm not putting that off for a robot. But I'd want one of us in something that doesn't vanish around 2039. If it's Dev with buses, fine, but I'd rather it was both of us.

say: **Ten years** is a long time in a supermarket; the layout has changed three times since I started.
There's time to **sort yourself out**, and I'd say that to colleagues.
think: She'd be **forty** when robots can do her job, and children would be small then.
Ten years makes it **tempting to drift**, which she calls the real trap.
do: Set a **deadline** to finish the pharmacy course by 2028.
Keep saving **three hundred** a month, aiming for six months' cushion before a baby.
Push for **supervisor** at Harlow's while keeping the steady wage.
feel: A nagging **fear of wasting** the decade, as she did with supervisor training.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like plenty, and four of my nine years at the supermarket went by while I was saying next year.
fieldNote: Fears **drift** more than the robots; knows her own habit of putting things off.
**Children** are planned anyway, which raises the stakes in the late 2030s.
Mood stays anxious because she still expects her **till job to go** with small children at home.

steps.text: Finish the pharmacy counter course by a fixed 2028 deadline
Save three hundred a month to reach six months before a baby
Keep the Harlow's wage and apply for supervisor every review

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because Dev and I would both be in trouble at nearly the same time and we'd have about four months of rent. What would help is Harlow's paying for courses before they need to, not after, and some help with rent while you retrain, because you can't do a course on thirty-two hours and still pay a landlord.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the customers. Half the people who come to my till are old, and the self-checkouts already confuse them. If all the people go, I don't know who helps old Frank, one of my regulars, find his banana.

headlineQuote: If all the people go, I don't know who helps old Frank, one of my regulars, find his banana.
portrait: Zoe, 27, has worked the **tills** at Harlow's supermarket for nine years and lives with Dev, a bus mechanic.
She already lived through one **automation wave** when self-checkouts cut the tills from fourteen to eight.
Practical and dry, she counts **hours and rent** more than she worries about headlines.
Her plan moves from the **pharmacy counter** to an electrical apprenticeship as the warning time shortens.
In the fastest picture she fears **both earners** losing work together and postpones the wedding.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and Dev could lose work together with about four months saved.
whatWouldHelp: Harlow's paying for **courses early**, before the jobs go.
**Rent help** while people retrain on reduced hours.
